summary: Clarifies the Domain Naming Convention for Internet user applications and explores what adopting it means for internet name service and user applications. It is explanatory rather than a protocol specification.

eli5.summary: A guide to how computer names should be built in layers, and what that means for programs that use the names.

questions: how do domain names resolve to addresses
subtitle: Building a hierarchical naming system for interconnected networks

tldr.problem: The early ARPANET used simple host names like ISIF, but as networks interconnected, a simple flat naming scheme could not scale or handle the administrative complexity of multiple independent organizations.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 819 proposes a hierarchical domain naming convention, where names are built like a tree from specific (leftmost) to general (rightmost): Fred@F.ISI.ARPA means user Fred in the ISI subdomain of the ARPA administrative domain. Each domain has a naming authority and name servers to translate names to addresses.
tldr.outcome: This hierarchical model became the foundation for the Internet DNS (Domain Name System). The RFC explains how decentralized naming authorities, multiple name server designs (iterative and recursive), and partial names work within this framework.

today: RFC 819 is not a standard; it is an explanatory memo that clarifies the Internet naming convention adopted by the community. The hierarchical domain model it describes became the foundation of the Domain Name System (DNS), formalized in later RFCs. The scheme has not been obsoleted and remains the basis of how names are organized on the modern Internet.

sections.title: From Flat Names to Hierarchical Domains
sections.content:
In the early ARPANET, the naming convention for mail was simple: user@host. As networks interconnected with other organizations, a central database of host names became unmanageable. RFC 819 introduces the Internet naming convention, which replaces the host field with a domain field built hierarchically.

The new format is user@host.domain.toplevel. For example, Fred@F.ISI.ARPA means user Fred at host F in the ISI subdomain of the ARPA domain. The name is absolute: it is fully qualified by reference to the root (right side is most general). This contrasts with relative naming schemes like UUCP, where a name like alpha!beta!gamma!john only makes sense if you know the starting point.

The RFC is explanatory rather than a formal standard; it clarifies the principles of hierarchical naming and explores the implications for name service, naming authorities, and applications.
sections.eli5: Old way: everyone in town is just "John". New way: John.Acme-Corp.Boston.USA. You look up John by finding Boston, then Acme-Corp, then John in that company.

sections.title: The Domain Hierarchy
sections.content:
The RFC models the domain hierarchy as a directed graph, specifically an in-tree rooted at a naming universe. Each node represents a domain. An arc from child domain B to parent domain A means B is a subdomain of A, and B's simple name is unique within A.

For any node, a simple name is unique within its parent. By concatenating a child's simple name with its parent's, uniqueness is preserved at the grandparent level. Continuing up the tree to the root ensures global uniqueness. For example, if a child's simple name is C1 and its parent is P1, then C1.P1 is unique at the grandparent level.

Within an endpoint domain (a leaf domain that represents a host or service), unique names are assigned to users, representing user mailboxes. The tree structure supports decentralization of naming authority: each domain can have its own naming authority and name servers, allowing growth and distribution of naming responsibility.

The RFC acknowledges anomalies: domains can have multiple parents (overlapping domains), which violates the strict tree structure. Such multi-parentage raises complex issues but is noted as a possibility for future exploration.
sections.eli5: Think of an organization chart. The root is the company. Below it are divisions, below those are departments, below those are teams, and finally individual people. Everyone's full address is their path from root to them.

sections.title: Absolute vs. Relative Naming and Advantages
sections.content:
The Internet naming convention is absolute naming: names are assigned with respect to a universal reference point (the naming universe root). An absolute name can be universally interpreted without context. This contrasts with relative naming, where a name's meaning depends on where you stand.

The RFC gives UUCP as an example of relative naming gone wrong. A message addressed as alpha!beta!gamma!john means: go to host alpha (which I know), from there go to beta, then gamma, then find john. But if the message is forwarded or a reply is sent, the frame of reference can be lost, breaking routing. Absolute names like john.gamma.beta.alpha.UUCP do not have this problem: they work from anywhere.

Absolute naming enables routing optimization, forwarding without ambiguity, and transparent interoperation across networks. It is the foundation of the Internet naming convention.
sections.eli5: Absolute name: the address on the envelope works anywhere because it tells the full path from the root office. Relative name: go left three houses and turn right—only works if you know where I am.

sections.title: Name Service and Name Servers
sections.content:
Name service translates names to network addresses. The hierarchical structure allows decentralized name service. Rather than one central database, each domain has one or more name servers.

The RFC describes two models for how a name server works. An iterative name server responds with either an address or the address of another name server to try next. The client must repeat the query with the new server until it gets an address. A recursive name server must do the work itself: if it cannot answer, it queries other servers on behalf of the client and returns a final address.

Clients must be prepared for either type. The basic name service at each domain translates simple names to addresses for all its child domains. If this is all, users would need to use fully qualified names always. To allow partial names (e.g., just "fred" instead of "fred.ISI.ARPA"), each domain's name service must also resolve simple names for its ancestors and their children. This requires a more sophisticated service, but it provides a better user experience.
sections.eli5: Iterative: you ask one office for directions, they point you to the next office, and you keep asking until you arrive. Recursive: you ask one office and they send a courier to find the person for you and report back.

sections.title: Naming Authority and Registration
sections.content:
Associated with each domain is a naming authority responsible for assigning simple names and ensuring uniqueness. Administratively, each domain has a registrar who maintains the naming authority.

The registrar of the naming universe (the root) designates the top-level domains (like ARPA) and appoints a registrar for each. Each registrar maintains the naming authority for their domain, assigning simple names to child domains and users. This hierarchical delegation of authority mirrors the domain hierarchy itself.

The RFC stresses that uniqueness of simple names within a subdomain is necessary to avoid ambiguity when partial names are used. A registrar must ensure that no two entities at the same level share a simple name.
sections.eli5: One mayor appoints city officials, who appoint neighborhood leads, who maintain the local phone book. Each one is responsible for keeping their level unique.

sections.title: Interoperability and Applications
sections.content:
The RFC addresses how applications like mail, file transfer (FTP), and terminal access (Telnet) use the naming system. For mail, user applications embed names in messages (e.g., the "From" and "To" fields). These names must remain valid if the message is forwarded to another recipient or quoted in a reply.

The hierarchical naming convention allows interoperability with foreign naming systems. A foreign system can be incorporated as a domain at any level. For example, a UUCP network can be added as a foreign domain: a UUCP address like alpha!beta!gamma!john becomes alpha!beta!gamma!john.UUCP in the Internet hierarchy. This makes it possible to mail from the Internet to UUCP without enforcing the Internet naming convention everywhere.

The RFC recommends that network-oriented applications provide a standard function or system call to translate Internet domain names to addresses, including local caching and querying name servers. This would give users a consistent interface across applications and networks.
sections.eli5: Just as you can write a letter to someone abroad with their foreign address plus your country's name appended, network systems can handle foreign naming schemes as special subdomains.

references.text: Postel, J., "Transmission Control Protocol", RFC 762, January 1980.
